> **Session focus:** *Educating collaborators, reporting of science, and framing researchable questions*

## Learning Objectives

* Teach statistical ideas to collaborators without losing nuance or trust
* Strengthen transparent reporting practices and replication mindset
* Frame researchable questions that align design, estimand, and analysis
* Integrate communication strategies with practical collaboration challenges

## Description of Activities

On 16 April (Block 2), we explored how to teach collaborators to communicate with statisticians, principles for reporting science, approaches for framing researchable questions, and perspectives on the “statistical pleasures” of medical collaborations. Activities emphasized bidirectional education and transparent, purpose-driven study design.

## Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

### 1. Description

We practiced teaching collaborators how to work with statisticians, reviewed principles for reporting science, and learned to frame researchable questions that connect purpose, design, and estimand. The sessions stressed reciprocity in education and transparency in methods and documentation.

### 2. Feelings

I felt encouraged that teaching is a learnable craft and relieved to have concrete approaches for difficult explanations. The reporting discussion heightened my sense of responsibility; small documentation choices can materially affect replicability and trust.

### 3. Evaluation

The bidirectional model (learn their clinical world; teach statistical thinking) felt practical and respectful. Reporting guidance was actionable—checklists and exemplars clarified expectations. I wished for more time to practice reframing vague questions into answerable ones with stakeholders in the room.

### 4. Analysis

ASCCR guided me to center Communication and Relationship: listening precedes explaining; partnership outruns service. Kolb’s cycle suggests repeated, low-stakes practice to internalize teaching skills. Double-loop learning shifted me from solution-first to question-first: if the question is mis-specified, excellent analysis still disappoints. Clear reporting operationalizes integrity.

### 5. Conclusion

Teaching, framing questions, and reporting are mutually reinforcing. They move collaborations from transactions to co-creation, anchoring rigor in shared understanding and transparent documentation.

### 6. Action Plan

I will prepare analogies and visuals for common concepts, adopt a reproducibility/reporting checklist, and develop a short “question-framing” guide (purpose, estimand, outcomes, design, constraints). I’ll schedule pre-meet reads of clinical background to align language and goals.
